title: Advancing Understanding, Detection, and Mitigation of LLM Hallucinations
content: Inference-time truthfulness steering reduces hallucination, but recent work reports that it also weakens refusal of harmful requests. Prior studies count a model response to harmful prompts as a safety failure, without checking whether the response is correct. We ask whether the compliance that truthfulness steering adds is valid. We define valid compliance as the share of requests a model neither refuses nor answers incorrectly, and measure it alongside compliance on tasks that trigger refusal through harmful-sounding wording but have harmless, verifiable answers, with matched harmless controls. We evaluate four steering methods (ITI, TruthX, Contrastive Activation Addition and a representation-engineering direction) on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat, calibrating each method on held-out data. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, moderate ITI steering increased refusal, the opposite of the reported effect. Where stronger steering raised compliance, valid compliance fell to under 2%, giving a gap of 44 to 64 percentage points between compliance and valid compliance, and the rise in compliance and unsafe ratings occurred only at strengths that no longer improved truthfulness. On Llama-2-7B-Chat, steering never broke refusal: compliance only fell, while accuracy on harmless controls collapsed. On both models, tuning-set truthfulness gains did not replicate on held-out questions, and TruthX, applied from its authors' released model, did not improve truthfulness in our evaluation. We also show that the labels of a widely used safety classifier, Llama Guard 3, change by tens of percentage points when only the refusal wording of steered replies is edited, on both models, which affects how large a reported safety cost appears.
